title: Reading a ball band
subtitle: How to extract hook size, gauge, weight, care, and fibre information from a yarn label
excerpt: The ball band is the primary information source for any yarn. Five pieces of information on the label tell you whether the yarn suits the project and how to care for the finished piece.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A batch number on the ball band identifying which production run the yarn came from. Yarn from the same dye lot is guaranteed to be the same colour; different lots may differ slightly.
The length of yarn in a ball or skein, stated in metres on the ball band.

content.text: The ball band carries everything you need to know before buying or working with a yarn: weight, fibre content, hook size, gauge,
, and care instructions. Reading it before you start prevents most common problems.

Weight and hook size: the recommended hook size (in mm) and the yarn weight category. The crochet hook symbol is a hook icon. The recommended hook is the starting point, not the final answer; check against the pattern's gauge.
Gauge: the number of stitches and rows per 10 cm using the stated hook and stitch (often double crochet or treble). This is the manufacturer's gauge, which gives a benchmark.
Fibre content: the percentage of each fibre in the blend. Determines care requirements and elasticity.
Care symbols: a set of small icons showing the recommended care method for the finished piece. The symbol with an X through it means do not do that thing.
Dye lot number: the batch code. Buy all balls for a project from the same lot. Keep one ball band per project until the piece is complete.
Tub with a number inside: machine wash at that temperature in degrees C.
Tub with a hand: hand wash only.
Square with a circle inside: tumble dry. Dots inside the circle indicate heat level (one dot = low, two = medium).
Iron symbol with dots: iron at the temperature shown by the number of dots.

items.symptom: The colour of two balls of the same yarn name and number looks slightly different in the finished piece
items.cause: The balls were from different dye lots.
items.fix: Check the lot number on each ball band. For future projects, buy all balls at once from the same lot. If one ball is a different lot, use it in a less visible section.

items.symptom: The ball band shows a knitting needle and gauge only, no crochet hook
items.cause: Some yarn bands include only knitting needle gauge. The crochet hook for that weight is usually one to two sizes larger than the knitting needle.
items.fix: Use the yarn weight category to find the standard crochet hook recommendation. A DK yarn typically uses a 4.0 mm crochet hook regardless of the knitting needle gauge shown.

content.text: Check the ball bands of any yarn you already own and note the fibre content, care symbols, and dye lot number. Store each band in a small project bag with the yarn so the information is there when needed.
